hints.content:
The graph of $y=\sqrt[3]{x}$ can be transformed
to get the graph of $y=-2\sqrt[3]{x-3}+2$. 
[[☃ explanation 1]]

options.explanation:
Suppose $f(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}$ and $g(x)=-2\sqrt[3]{x-3}+2$.  

>$\begin{align}f(x)&=\sqrt[3]{x}\\\\
f(x-3)&=\sqrt[3]{x-3}\\\\
-2f(x-3)&=-2\sqrt[3]{x-3}\\\\
-2f(x-3)+2&=-2\sqrt[3]{x-3}+2\\\\
\end{align}$

Notice that what is on the right-hand side of the equal sign is $g(x)$.  Therefore, $g(x)=-2f(x-3)+2$.  

Since function $g$ can be built from function $f$, the graph of function $g$ is a transformation of the graph of function $f$.

hints.content:
Replacing $x$ with $x-3$ shifts the graph of $y=\sqrt[3]{x}$ right $3$ units.


[[☃ image 1]]

options.alt: A cube root function graph and its shifted graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has a middle point at (zero, zero) and passes through (negative eight, negative two) and (eight, two). The shifted graph has a middle point at (three, zero) and passes through (negative five, negative two) and (eleven, two).

hints.content:
Multiplying $\sqrt[3]{x-3}$ by $-2$ reflects the graph of $y=\sqrt[3]{x-3}$ across the $x$-axis and stretches it vertically by a factor of $2$.

[[☃ image 1]]

Note that the graph of the function passes through $(2,-1)$ *before* the transformation, and $(2, 2 )$ *after* the transformation.  This is because each $y$-coordinate is multiplied by $-2$.

options.alt: A cube root function graph and its transformed graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has a middle point at (three, zero) and passes through (negative five, negative two) and (eleven, two). The transformed graph has a middle point at (three, zero) and passes through (negative five, four) and (eleven, negative four).

hints.content:
Adding $2$ to the function shifts the graph of $y=-2\sqrt[3]{x-3}$ up $2$ units.

[[☃ image 1]]

Note that it is important to follow order of operations when building the function, as function transformations are not always commutative.  [[☃ explanation 1]]

options.explanation:
Consider the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$.

If we shift the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$ down $2$ units, and then reflect this across the $x$-axis, we get the following graph.

![A square root function graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has an endpoint (zero, two) and passes through (ten, negative one).](web+graphie:${☣ LOCALPATH}/images/838d19b306cd3a25ac6c67be671bb6a26eaf0e71)

However, if we first reflect the graph of $y=\sqrt{x}$ across the $x$-axis and then shift this graph down $2$ units, we get the following graph.

![A square root function graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has an endpoint (zero, negative two) and passes through (ten, negative five).](web+graphie:${☣ LOCALPATH}/images/76bbee52d28bfb5f5bcd72a6831a797eaab9824d)

These graphs are not the same, indicating that the order in which you perform the transformations is important!

options.alt: A cube root function graph and its shifted graph on an x y coordinate plane. It has a middle point at (three, zero) and passes through (negative five, four) and (eleven, negative four). The shifted graph has a middle point at (three, two) and passes through (negative five, six) and (eleven, negative two).
